R03.answer:
1. The animation shows how inflation wears down what a fixed-dollar income can buy. Three illustrative retirees, Edna, Ruth and Carl, each start a 20-year retirement at a different point in US history: Jan 1949, Aug 2006 and Jan 1966. Each gets the same 2% annual raise. The label "US consumer prices (CPI-U)" shows the inflation data comes from the US consumer price index.

2. Each person starts with a full row of crates, which stands for their purchasing power. Over the 20 years, the rows shrink by different amounts. By year 20, Edna still has all 10 crates. Ruth has about 9. Carl has only about 4.

3. The same 2% raise protects against inflation very differently depending on when someone retires. Edna's era had mild inflation, so her income kept up. Ruth's era had somewhat faster inflation, so she lost a little. Carl retired in 1966, just before a period of high inflation, so his 2% raise fell far behind and his buying power dropped by more than half. The footers say "US only · history, not a forecast" and "ILLUSTRATIVE", so these are past examples and not predictions.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that a fixed 2% raise is not guaranteed to keep up with inflation. For someone comparing two payout options, that could mean checking whether each option adjusts for inflation, and how much. The animation says nothing about which option to choose.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the outcomes for the three retirees. It doesn't mention annuities or payout options, and it makes no recommendation.

The animation does not say which option to pick, and it does not say that inflation will repeat the worst case.
